# Energy balance

> *Body weight follows the gap between the energy we take in and the energy we spend. That gap is
> not free to move: when intake falls for long enough, energy expenditure falls too, narrowing it.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Break total energy expenditure into basal metabolic rate, the thermic effect of food and physical
  activity, and explain what drives each.
- Estimate a person's energy needs with the Mifflin–St Jeor equation and a physical-activity level,
  and explain why the result is only a starting point.
- Compare BMI, waist circumference, bioelectrical impedance and DXA by what each measures, how it
  is used and its limits.
- Explain how calorimetry, doubly labelled water and the respiratory quotient measure energy
  expenditure and the fuel being burned.
- Explain how adaptive thermogenesis and leptin signalling oppose changes in body weight.
- Relate Singapore's food environment to energy balance, and name the practical levers that shift it.
:::

## Energy balance at a glance {#sec-overview}

**Energy balance** is the relationship between the energy taken in as food and drink and the energy
the body spends. When intake exceeds expenditure, the surplus is stored, mostly as fat; when
expenditure exceeds intake, the body draws on its stores. Sustained in either direction, the
imbalance shifts body weight and metabolic health.

As an equation, energy balance looks simple:

$$ \text{energy stored} = \text{energy in} - \text{energy out} $$

The "out" side, the **total energy expenditure (TEE)**, has three parts: the basal metabolic rate
(BMR), the thermic effect of food (TEF) and physical activity (PA):

$$ \text{TEE} = \text{BMR} + \text{TEF} + \text{PA} $$

The two sides of the first equation are not independent, however. When intake falls for long enough,
the "out" side falls to meet it, so body weight does not behave like a simple bank balance (see
[Metabolic adaptation after weight loss](#sec-defended)).

::: {.callout-note}
## Small numbers, long time
A daily surplus of about 100 kcal, roughly one sweetened drink, is enough to add meaningful weight
over a year if nothing else changes [@hill2003energygap]. The smallness is also the good news: small,
sustainable changes are the practical lever in counselling, because energy balance plays out over
months, not meals.
:::

## Energy expenditure: the "out" side {#sec-out}

### The three parts of expenditure {#sec-expenditure}

Most of the energy the body spends goes on keeping it alive at rest. **Basal metabolic rate (BMR)**
is the energy needed to keep the body running at complete rest: heartbeat, breathing, kidneys and the
constant turnover of cells. It is the largest component, typically 60–70% of TEE. BMR is driven
mainly by **fat-free (lean) mass**, the body mass other than fat, because its muscle and organs are
metabolically active while stored fat is much less so. BMR falls with age, partly as lean mass is
lost; it is lower when thyroid hormone is low; and it differs between the sexes largely because
body composition does [@westerterp2017dlw].

The **thermic effect of food (TEF)** is the energy cost of digesting, absorbing and processing a
meal, about 10% of TEE [@westerterp2004dit]. Protein costs more to process than carbohydrate or fat, which is one reason protein-rich meals
feel more satisfying (see the [*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-satiety)
chapter).

**Physical activity (PA)** is the most variable component: it differs most between two otherwise
similar people, and it is the component most under a person's control. It has two parts:

Exercise activity
: Deliberate exercise, such as a run, a gym session or a swim.

Non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT)
: The energy spent on all other movement, such as walking to the hawker centre, fidgeting, taking
  the stairs and standing. NEAT varies enormously between people and, over a day, can outweigh
  formal exercise entirely [@levine2002neat].

### Estimating BMR: the Mifflin–St Jeor equation {#sec-bmr}

Because BMR is the largest component, estimating a person's needs starts with estimating it. The
widely used **Mifflin–St Jeor equation** estimates BMR from weight ($W$, kg), height ($H$, cm), age
($A$, years) and sex [@mifflin1990]:

$$ \text{BMR}_{\text{women}} = 10W + 6.25H - 5A - 161 $$
$$ \text{BMR}_{\text{men}} = 10W + 6.25H - 5A + 5 $$

To estimate total daily needs, BMR is multiplied by a **physical-activity level (PAL)** factor:
roughly 1.4 for a sedentary person, 1.6 for a lightly active one, 1.75 for a moderately active one
and 2.0 for a very active one.

$$ \text{TEE} \approx \text{BMR} \times \text{PAL} $$

Enter a person's details and activity level below to see how the daily total splits into BMR, TEF
and activity, and how far the activity factor moves it.

<div data-island="energy-budget" data-src="/diagrams/energy-budget.yml"></div>

::: {.example}
A sedentary woman aged 52 weighs 68 kg and is 157 cm tall:
$\text{BMR} = 10(68) + 6.25(157) - 5(52) - 161 \approx 1{,}240$ kcal/day, and her total needs are
$\approx 1{,}240 \times 1.4 \approx 1{,}740$ kcal/day.
:::

The equations are population estimates. They set a sensible starting point for one person but do
not measure that person's needs. For weight loss, Singapore's obesity guideline starts from a deficit of at least 500 kcal/day below these estimated needs, with loss preferably no faster than 0.5–1 kg a week [@hpbmoh2016obesityCPG].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: two women weigh the same, but one carries far more muscle. Why is her BMR likely to be higher?
BMR is driven mainly by lean mass, because muscle and organs are metabolically active while stored fat
is much less so. At the same weight, the more muscular woman carries more metabolically active
tissue, so she spends more energy at rest.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why is the estimate of 1,740 kcal/day for the sedentary woman in the example only a starting point?
The Mifflin–St Jeor equation is a population estimate: it predicts BMR from weight, height, age and
sex, so it cannot see how much of her weight is lean mass, the main driver of BMR. Physical activity,
the most variable component, enters only as a rough PAL band.
:::

## Measuring body composition and energy expenditure {#sec-measuring}

Energy needs track **body composition**, what the weight is made of. Two people of the same weight
can differ completely in how much of it is muscle and how much is fat, and that difference changes
both their BMR and their health risk. Four tools for screening or measuring body composition are
compared below, from cheap, rough screening to the accurate reference standard:

| Tool | What it measures | Use and limits |
|---|---|---|
| Body mass index (BMI) | Weight ÷ height² | Cheap population screening, not a body-fat measurement; cannot tell muscle from fat |
| Waist circumference | Central (visceral) fat, stored around the abdomen | Adds the central-fat risk that BMI misses |
| Bioelectrical impedance (BIA) | Fat versus lean, estimated from a tiny electrical current | Convenient (the "body-fat" bathroom scales) but easily thrown off by hydration |
| DXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry), a low-dose X-ray scan | Fat versus lean | The accurate clinical and research reference |

BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so it misclassifies the very muscular and can miss excess fat in
people who are slim by weight. BMI is therefore a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Asian cut-offs for overweight are set lower than the international ones, because the risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease rises at a lower BMI in Asian populations [@whoExpert2004AsianBMI] (see the [*Obesity & metabolic syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd) chapter). Waist circumference captures
**central (visceral) fat**, the fat stored around the abdomen. That fat carries more metabolic risk
than fat on the hips and thighs, so the waist measurement adds what BMI misses [@whoWaist2011].

Energy expenditure itself is measured with research tools. BMR is measured by **calorimetry**,
directly from the heat the body produces or indirectly from the oxygen it consumes and the carbon
dioxide it produces. Total expenditure in free-living people (those going about their normal lives)
is measured with **doubly labelled water**, a harmless isotope tracer followed over one to two weeks;
it is the gold standard behind the expenditure shares given earlier [@westerterp2017dlw]. In the
clinic, the estimating equations do the everyday work.

The gases measured in indirect calorimetry also show which fuel the body is burning. The
**respiratory quotient (RQ)** is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed: about 1.0
when burning carbohydrate and about 0.7 when burning fat, with a mixed diet around 0.85 [@rqValuesStd]. RQ shifts as
the body moves between the fed and fasted states (see the
[*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-rq) chapter).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient's BMI is in the healthy range, but her waist circumference is large. Why does the waist measurement change the picture?
BMI uses only weight and height, so it cannot tell muscle from fat and can miss excess fat in people
who are slim by weight. Waist circumference captures central (visceral) fat, which carries more
metabolic risk than fat on the hips and thighs. Her large waist flags a risk that her BMI misses.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can indirect calorimetry show which fuel the body is burning, as well as how much energy it spends?
Indirect calorimetry measures the oxygen consumed and the carbon dioxide produced. Their ratio, the
respiratory quotient, differs by fuel: about 1.0 when carbohydrate is burned and about 0.7 when fat
is burned, with a mixed diet near 0.85. One set of gas measurements therefore gives both the energy
spent and the fuel mix.
:::

## Metabolic adaptation after weight loss {#sec-defended}

Energy balance is actively regulated, not free to drift. Two physiological responses oppose
changes in body weight: a fall in energy expenditure after weight loss, and signalling of the size
of the fat stores to the brain (see the
[*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-defended) chapter).

When someone loses weight, "energy out" falls by more than their smaller body should require. This
extra drop, **adaptive thermogenesis** (also called metabolic adaptation), makes lost weight easy to
regain. Hunger also rises after weight loss and is still raised a year later [@sumithran2011hormonal]. Together with the leptin signal below, these compensatory responses actively oppose weight
change, and they appear to oppose loss more strongly than gain [@schwartz2017obesity]. That
compensation helps explain why "just eat less" so often fails in the long term [@leibel1995energy; @sumithran2011hormonal].

Adipose tissue also signals to the brain how much fat is stored. It releases a hormone, **leptin**,
in rough proportion to the amount of fat carried [@considine1996leptin]. The brain uses leptin as a long-term signal of fat
stores, often likened to a fuel gauge, to regulate appetite and body weight over months and years.
If leptin signals a large store, extra leptin might be expected to cut appetite and weight. Simply
giving it does not, however, reverse common obesity [@heymsfield1999recombinant]; the reason is
taken up under leptin in the
[*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-leptin) chapter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: after losing weight, a patient eats to an energy estimate calculated for her new, lower weight. Why does the weight tend to return?
After weight loss, expenditure falls by more than the smaller body should require (adaptive
thermogenesis), so an estimate based on her new weight is likely to overstate what she now spends and
can leave her in surplus. Her smaller fat stores also release less leptin, the long-term signal of
their size, so the brain registers a smaller store, and appetite rises, favouring regain.
Energy balance is actively regulated, not free, and the compensation opposes loss more strongly than
gain.
:::

## Is body weight just calories in minus out? {#sec-close}

Partly. The equation is real: energy that was never eaten cannot be stored, and a sustained deficit
does lower weight. The two sides are linked, however. When intake falls, energy expenditure falls
too, and body fat releases leptin in rough proportion to its size, a signal
the brain uses to regulate body weight. The rule "calories in minus calories out" is therefore the
right *bookkeeping* and a poor *strategy*, because the "out" column itself shifts in response to
intake (see the [*Appetite and weight regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-defended)
chapter).

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Singapore's food environment tilts the balance toward the "in" side, quietly and by default. Eating
out is the norm: about three in four adults usually eat at least one of their daily meals out [@naidoo2017eatingout]. Hawker and food-court favourites are energy-dense
(high in kcal for their weight). A plate of *char kway teow* with a sweet drink can carry a large
share of a day's energy in one sitting, and the drink alone can add a couple of hundred easily missed
kcal. A largely sedentary, air-conditioned, car-and-MRT lifestyle keeps the
activity side low, with little of the NEAT that a more walking-dependent city would provide.

The festive calendar adds to the surplus. Chinese New Year, Hari Raya, Deepavali and Christmas each
bring days of feasting. The modest weight gained across a year of such occasions is not fully lost
afterwards, so it accumulates over the years [@yanovski2000holiday]. None of this is a moral failing;
it is an environment that keeps "energy in" easy and "energy out" low.

The National Nutrition Survey shows a gap between the guidelines and the plate [@mohNNS2022]. Three
practical levers aim to close that gap without calorie counting:

- My Healthy Plate (¼ wholegrains, ¼ protein, ½ fruit and vegetables; see the
  [*Why nutrition matters*](01-why-nutrition-matters.qmd) chapter) lowers a meal's energy density
  [@hpbHealthyPlate].
- Nutri-Grade flags the sugary drinks that are the easiest surplus to cut.
- Everyday movement (stairs over the escalator, a walk after dinner, alighting a stop early)
  adds back the NEAT that city life removes.
